verses.1: Al-Mizan takes the verse to mean: “This is the Book gradually sent-down from Allah, the All-mighty, the All-wise.” Tanzīl functions as a passive description of the Book, while min Allāh qualifies its gradual sending-down. The alternative analysis, in which “the gradual sending-down of the Book” is the subject and “from Allah” its predicate, is considered less plausible.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains that inzāl is used here rather than tanzīl because the verse concerns the Book as a whole sent down to the Prophet with the truth, whereas tanzīl signifies its revelation in parts. Bi al-ḥaqq means that the Book came accompanied by truth; consequently, its command to worship Allah with exclusive faith is itself true and binding.

In this context, dīn means ʿibāda, though it may also denote one’s whole way of life. Worship is the practice of servanthood (ʿubūdiyya) according to God’s prescribed way, so exclusive faith requires displaying servanthood in every aspect of life by adhering to His ordinances.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse publicly generalizes the preceding command: exclusive faith belongs to Allah alone and is obligatory for everyone who receives this summons. Allah accepts neither worship combined with worship of others nor worship directed to others alone.

Those who take awliyāʾ besides Him take them as arbāb: rulers and governors of the world’s affairs. The idolaters held that God was too exalted to be directly comprehended or worshipped, so they sought nearness through created intermediaries—angels, jinns, and holy persons—whom they considered true lords and deities. They worshipped these beings to gain benefit, repel harm, give thanks for blessings, obtain intercession, and be brought near to God. Though they held God to be the Creator and originator, the Lord of Lords and God of Gods, they assigned worldly governance to these other beings. Thus their association was not a claim that the associates shared in creating or originating the cosmos, a claim neither idolaters nor monotheists made.

Physical idols of wood, stone, and other materials were originally representations of such spiritual lords, not themselves lords or deities. But ignorant worshippers confused the representations with what they represented. Al-Mizan identifies this confusion among pre-Islamic Arabs and uneducated Sabaean laypersons, who likewise failed to distinguish star-idols, stars, and the spirits regarded by the Sabaean priesthood as the true lords and gods.

The statement “We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah” expounds their taking guardians besides Him and states their justification: by worshipping these deities, they claim to approach Allah. This turning from God to others is why they are mushrikūn: they assign others lordship and divinity over this world while reserving supreme lordship and divinity for God over those associates.

Al-Mizan notes two readings of “Allah will indeed judge between them”: the pronoun may refer to the idolaters and their guardians, or, more fittingly to the context, to the idolaters and the monotheists who devoted faith exclusively to Allah. “Allah does not guide someone who is a liar and an ingrate” means that His final judgment will be against the disbelievers, leading them to hell. A kaffār is either exceedingly ungrateful for God’s blessings or one who excessively covers the truth, and guidance here means being conveyed to a good final outcome.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as a refutation of every claim that Allah has a son, including the idolaters’ claim about daughters, the Christian proclamation that Jesus is the Son of God, and the Qur’an’s report concerning Ezra—though the latter apparently meant an honorific rather than a metaphysical sonship. In either form, sonship entails association with God. A real son would derive from the father and share his essence, attributes, and effects; an adopted or figurative son would share the father’s rank, authority, dominion, nobility, and some rules of lineage. Both are impossible for Allah.

The particle law in “Had Allah intended to take a son” marks an impossible supposition. If He had so intended, He could have chosen whomever He wished from His creation; “from those He has created” establishes that the supposed choice would be other than Him. But “Immaculate is He! He is Allah, the One, the All-paramount” denies the antecedent and therefore also its consequence. Allah is one in essence, with nothing sharing or resembling it; one in His essential attributes, such as life, knowledge, and power, which are identical with His essence; and one in the affairs flowing from His essence, including creation, sovereignty, might, and greatness. As All-paramount, He dominates all things, while every being is dependent, humbled, and within His dominion.

Thus the argument is: if Allah intended a son, He would choose one from creation; but His oneness and paramountness make such an intention impossible; therefore, choosing a son is impossible. Al-Mizan rejects a more elaborate reading, apparently derived from al-Zamakhsharī’s al-Kashshāf, which treats God’s special choosing of creatures, especially angels, as the source of the error that they are His offspring. The verse’s context and tone do not support that explanation, and it does not refute those who call a creature God’s adopted or honorific son precisely because He chose that creature. Other proposed readings lack merit.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan considers it likely that the verse’s account of creation and governance expounds Allah’s All-paramountness. Yet its close connection with the following verse suggests a new argument for His exclusive lordship. Since the idolaters could affirm one Creator while positing many lords and deities, the Qur’an joins creation to cosmic governance to show that tadbīr is not separate from khalq: each is an aspect of the other. Hence governance belongs exclusively to Allah just as creation does.

“He created the heavens and the earth with truth” means that creation is purposeful rather than vain and is directed to the Resurrection. “He winds the night over the day, and winds the day over the night” is a metaphor for their uninterrupted succession, each following the other through divine governance. The sun and moon are subjected to the cosmic order and move until a fixed term they cannot exceed.

The ending may indicate that these signs establish Allah’s sole worthiness of worship: the All-mighty is never subdued, whereas others are needy and sometimes overcome; the All-forgiver alone can forgive sins. It may also encourage faith in Him: through His might believers become mighty, and through faith in the All-forgiver they receive forgiveness.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan states that the verse addresses all humanity. “A single soul” refers, in light of similar verses, to Adam, while its mate is his wife, created from the same human species; thumma indicates an interval between the two. Humanity thus became abundant from this pair.

The eight mates of cattle are the male and female of camels, cows, sheep, and goats. Their coming into existence on earth is called inzāl because things emerge from God’s treasuries and the unseen into the visible realm: “There is not a thing but that its sources are with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure (15:21).”

“Creation after creation” describes the successive stages of human formation in the mothers’ wombs. The direct address especially concerns beings endowed with intellect. The threefold darkness is, according to some and a narration from Imam al-Bāqir in Majmaʿ al-bayān, that of the stomach, womb, and amniotic sac. The alternative of the loins, womb, and embryonic sac is rejected, since the verse places these darknesses within the mothers’ wombs, not men’s loins.

The One whose creation and governance have been described is therefore Allah alone, the Lord: a lord is the sovereign who governs the affairs of his domain. All sovereignty in this world and the hereafter belongs exclusively to Him. His exclusive divinity follows from His exclusive lordship, for a deity is worshipped as the lord who governs servants’ affairs and is feared, hoped in, or thanked. The final question reproaches those who turn from worshipping their Creator, Governor, and sovereign Master to worship others.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah’s summons to monotheism and exclusive faith does not arise from any need for human worship. Faith and obedience add nothing to Him, and disbelief and disobedience harm Him in no way, for benefit and harm concern contingent, needy beings, whereas the Necessary Existent is self-sufficient in His essence. The summons instead expresses divine solicitude for human happiness in this world and the next, just as His provision of blessings serves their welfare.

The ingratitude mentioned here is kufr al-niʿma, ingratitude for God’s blessings, and corresponds to disbelief just as shukr corresponds to faith. Though Allah needs no one, He does not approve of this ingratitude because all people are His servants, subject to His dominion and immersed in His blessings. Servanthood does not permit a servant to forget his master’s authority, choose another master, disobey his master in obedience to His enemy, or be ungrateful for His kindness. Conversely, He approves thanksgiving and exclusive faith for His servants.

“His servants” is universal, not limited to the devoted (mukhliṣūn) or sin-protected (maʿṣūmūn), as some commentators, including al-Zamakhsharī, propose from (15:42). That interpretation would imply that Allah approves the disbelievers’ disbelief, make the call to monotheism pointless, and needlessly single out prophets or similarly protected servants even though their gratitude is already included among what Allah approves.

No one bears another’s deeds or is punished for a sin not committed. All return to their Lord, who will disclose the reality of what they did and judge them with full knowledge of what their hearts contain.

Al-Mizan further explains that riḍā, approval or satisfaction, and its opposite sukhṭ, displeasure, are affirmative states applicable to sentient, free-willed beings. Approval normally concerns qualities and acts, not entities except from a particular perspective connected with the Hereafter. It differs from willing (irāda): approval is fixed upon something after it has occurred, or is supposed to have occurred, and is a state in the approver rather than in its object.

Because approval accompanies an occurring thing, it cannot be an essential divine attribute (ṣifat al-dhāt), since God’s essence is not a locus of change. Divine approval is instead an attribute of action (ṣifat al-fiʿl), like mercy, wrath, willing, and disliking. For Allah to approve something means that it accords with His action. Since His actions are natural (takwīnī) and moral (tashrīʿī), approval likewise has these two senses: every natural phenomenon that He wills and brings about receives His natural approval as His own action, while faith and righteous deeds receive His moral approval because they conform to His moral commands. What opposes those commands, such as disbelief and immorality, never receives His moral approval.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan says that the verse exposes the human predisposition to ingratitude despite innate knowledge of God through fiṭra. When distress comes, a person acknowledges God’s lordship, turns penitently to Him, excludes all others, and begs for relief. Yet when God grants the blessing of deliverance, he becomes occupied with it and forgets the very distress for which he had earlier appealed.

The preferred reading of mā kāna yadʿū ilayh is that mā is relative and refers to the prior distress, while ilayh means “for which.” The alternatives—that mā is gerundival and refers to former supplications to God, or that the person forgets God Himself—are less likely, especially the last.

By setting up andād, a person assigns equals to Allah in lordship and divinity and thereby leads people from His way, since people imitate those in authority and can be led astray by conduct as well as speech. Although andād may refer to idols and false deities, Al-Mizan considers it more likely to include everything on which people rely instead of Allah, an interpretation that applies beyond idolaters even though disbelievers are the verse’s focus.

“Revel in your ingratitude for a while” is not permission but a threat and foretelling: temporary enjoyment cannot prevent one destined for hellfire from entering it.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan connects the verse to the principle that no bearer bears another’s burden: the ungrateful and the thankful will not be treated alike. The question leaves its contrasting half implicit: is the disbeliever destined for hellfire equal to one who is continuously obedient and humble before his Lord in the night, alternately prostrating and standing, fearing the punishment of the Hereafter while hoping for His mercy? They are not equal.

Qunūṭ means persistent obedience and humility, and ānāʾ means moments or watches of the night. Fear and hope are joined here, though the mercy hoped for is not explicitly confined to the Hereafter and may perhaps encompass this world as well.

“Are those who know equal to those who do not know?” concerns knowledge of God, through which a human being reaches completion and receives true benefit; its absence is truly harmful. Other kinds of knowledge resemble worldly wealth, useful only while the world endures. Those who possess intellect take admonition by reflecting on realities; those who do not therefore cannot be equal to those who know.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan holds that “in this world” qualifies “those who do good”: those who continually do good in this life will receive unqualified good. Because the promised good is unrestricted, it includes both worldly and otherworldly good. In this world, faith and righteous conduct bring a happy heart, a healthy spirit, and protection from the confusion, inner conflict, anxiety, and helplessness of those who lack faith and find themselves subject to forces beyond their control; they also bring eternal happiness and lasting comfort. The alternative reading, which confines the promise to good in this world, is rejected.

“Allah’s earth is vast” encourages believers to emigrate when persecution makes remaining in Mecca difficult, yet its wording establishes a universal maxim rather than a rule confined to the Prophet’s time. The interpretation that it refers to the spaciousness of paradise is unlikely.

The restriction in “Only the patient will be paid in full their reward without any reckoning” applies to “without any reckoning.” The patient will receive all that is due to them without being called to account, having their records opened, or having reward measured according to their deeds. Ṣābirūn is unrestricted: it includes patience in obedience, in avoiding sin, and in hardship, although the context especially suggests endurance of worldly hardship and persecution for faith, exclusive devotion, and Godwariness. The alternative that “without any reckoning” merely describes an abundant reward is less accurate.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan reads these verses as a recapitulation of the opening command, “Indeed We have sent down the Book to you with the truth; so worship Allah, putting exclusive faith in Him (39:2).” The Prophet is commanded to announce this so that the people know they cannot induce him to abandon his mission or approve their association of partners with God.

The command to worship God sincerely is not merely addressed to the Prophet as an indirect way of commanding his audience; he himself, like them, is commanded to worship God and devote faith exclusively to Him. Moreover, he must be the first to submit to the revelation and believe in it before conveying it to others. Thus he calls others only to what he has first accepted, fears his Lord, worships sincerely regardless of their response, and will not change. His command also has this additional aspect: although he shares their duty, it was directed to him first so that he would be first to submit.

Al-Mizan says that whether the lām in li-an akūna is taken as explanatory—submission is characterized by his being first—or as superfluous, as its omission in Say, ‘I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit’ (6:14) has led some to say, the resulting sense is the same: his priority in submission either describes it or is its purpose. Al-Zamakhsharī, in al-Kashshāf, proposes that the Prophet is first among his contemporaries and people to submit; first to call them to submit; first to call himself to what he calls others; an exemplar whose deeds accord with his words rather than a ruler who commands what he does not do; or a model of submission for others. Al-Mizan judges the third meaning most fitting to the context.

verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that disobeying the Lord here means contravening His command to worship Him with exclusive faith, and that the tremendous day is the Day of Resurrection. The verse prepares for what follows.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan says that the Prophet’s declaration, “Only Allah do I worship,” explicitly confirms his obedience to God and denies any hope that he will disobey Him. The fronting of the object expresses exclusivity (ḥaṣr), reinforced by “putting my exclusive faith in Him.” “So worship whatever you wish besides Him” is a threat: their false objects of worship will not benefit them, and they will bear the consequence of turning from exclusive worship of God.

The losers on the Day of Resurrection lose their capital; khusrān expresses loss more emphatically than khusr. To lose oneself is to expose it to misery, depriving it of its capacity for perfection and happiness until it has no hope of happiness; losing one’s family is comparable. The address thus warns idolaters that their disbelief endangers themselves and that, by prompting their nearest people toward disbelief and idolatry, they also cause their loss.

This is manifest loss because worldly losses are temporary and may be recovered or replaced, whereas the loss of oneself on the Day of Judgment is permanent and unending. Al-Mizan’s initial explanation takes ahl to mean one’s closest people in this world. Some, however, take it to mean the wives, servants, and other blessings prepared in paradise for a believer who acts righteously. They consider this more suitable because worldly kinship and social ties are severed on that day: “there will be no ties between them on that day (23:101),” and “It is a day when no soul will be of any avail to another soul (82:19).” They also cite the return of one given his record in the right hand to “his folks joyfully (84:7–9).”

verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that ẓilal, the plural of ẓulla, denotes canopies or, as some say, elevated coverings. Canopies of fire above and below show that the people of the Fire are wholly surrounded by flames; this threat is meant to deter God’s servants and make them wary of Him.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan reports al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī’s definition of al-ṭāghūt, “the Rebel,” as anything invoked or worshipped apart from God, a term usable in either singular or plural. In this context it means idols and every false deity. Those promised good news must not only refrain from worshipping ṭāghūt but also turn penitently to Allah: rejecting false gods must be joined to the positive worship of God, which is exclusive faith in Him.

The wording “My servants,” rather than simply “them,” both honors these people and introduces their description as those who listen to the word and follow its best part. Since following concerns practice, the best part of the word is what guides most fully to truth and gives the most useful counsel. Such people are disposed to seek truth, guidance, and the reality of things: between truth and falsehood, or guidance and error, they choose the former; and between what is true and truer, or good guidance and better guidance, they choose what is truer and better. They listen without rejecting a word merely because it is unfamiliar or contrary to desire, pondering and understanding it in the hope of finding any truth it contains and fearing to miss it.

Al-Mizan rejects as arbitrary specifications, unsupported by any specifier, the views that they hear all words but follow only the Qur’an, or that they hear God’s commands and choose the better permitted option, such as forgiveness rather than retribution (qiṣāṣ), or secret rather than open charity. Their truth-seeking readiness is itself a form of general divine guidance, from which specific guidance to divine teachings proceeds. Lubb, here equivalent to ʿaql, is the faculty by which a human being is guided to truth; possessing intellect is marked by following truth and thereby following God’s religion.

verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that for the word of punishment to become due against someone is for disbelief to make entry into Hell necessary, as in “But those who are faithless and deny Our signs, they shall be the inmates of the Fire and they shall remain in it forever (2:39).” In context, “Can you rescue someone who is in the Fire?” means: can you save one against whom the punishment has become due?

This is preferable to taking the first question as a comparison between one destined for punishment and one entitled to paradise. Another interpretation takes the doubled interrogation and the expression “someone who is in the Fire” in place of a pronoun as emphatic: can one whose punishment has become due be saved from the Fire? The view that an omitted pronoun makes the meaning “Can you rescue one of them who is in the Fire?” is the weakest interpretation.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that ghuruf, the plural of ghurfa, are elevated homes. Some interpret the lofty abodes built above one another as contrasting with the faithless being enclosed by “canopies of fire above them, and canopies beneath them (39:16).”

“A promise of Allah” means that God has promised these abodes; waʿd Allāh functions as an absolute object in place of the verbal statement that God has made this promise. “Allah does not break His promise” states the divine custom concerning promises and reassures the Qur’an’s audience.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that God sends rain into the earth’s springs and watercourses, which carry it like veins, then brings forth crops of varying colours before they wither, yellow, and become debris. Al-Ṭabrisī defines yanābīʿ as places from which water issues, zarʿ as plants without trunks, and huṭam as pieces of hay and grass. This changing cycle is an admonition for people of intellect and an argument for God’s sole lordship (rubūbiyya) over the cosmos.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan takes “remembrance of God” (dhikr Allāh) to mean the preceding reminder in the signs of rain and vegetation. Those who are guided differ from the astray because they follow a light from their Lord and have receptive rather than obstinate hearts, enabling them to recognize and accept the best word.

The verse’s implicit rhetorical comparison asks whether one whose breast has been opened to Islam can be like one with a hardened heart; it denies that they are alike. sharḥ al-ṣadr means expanding the breast to encompass what it receives. Openness to Islam—submission to God’s will, which is truth—does not mean uncomprehending acceptance: one accepts the truth through discerning it as true guidance. Being “upon” a light portrays the person as travelling by that light, perceiving truth and distinguishing it from falsehood; the astray person’s constricted breast lacks this light and this capacity.

Hardness of heart entails a contracted breast and absence of guiding light. Such people do not reflect on God’s signs and consequently are not guided to the truth they indicate; hence they are in manifest error. The verse thus defines guidance by its consequence, openness of breast and being upon light from the Lord, and misguidance by its converse, a heart hardened against God’s remembrance.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as an explanation of the Qur’an’s guidance. The Qur’an is the best discourse because it contains pure truth, inaccessible to falsehood. Its being mutashābih means that its parts resemble and conform to one another, not that the whole text is ambiguous in the sense opposed to muḥkam. Its mathānī are verses joined to, referring to, clarifying, and explaining one another without conflict or contradiction.

The clause about skins quivering describes the scripture: those who fear their Lord hear His speech, attend to His greatness and magnificence, and are overcome with fear, so that their skins contract and tremble. Their hearts are not said to quiver, since “hearts” here means souls, which feel fear but do not quiver. Thereafter their skins and hearts soften—that is, become still and tranquil in God’s remembrance, receptive of it and at peace with it.

This movement from fearful trembling to tranquillity is itself Allah’s guidance, defined through its consequence. God guides by His grace those servants who have retained their receptivity to guidance and are not diverted by impediments such as sinfulness and wrongdoing; no obligation compels Him to guide anyone.

Some commentators take “That” to refer to the Qur’an and infer that the verses establish that guidance belongs exclusively to God. Al-Mizan rejects that inference from these verses, while affirming the proposition itself: guidance originally belongs wholly to God and belongs to chosen servants only derivatively, not as something they earn. He bestows it either directly or through divinely guided intermediaries. Thus one whom God leaves astray by not granting guidance, directly or through an intermediary, has no guide.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as a rhetorical comparison between one who suffers punishment on the Day of Resurrection—the one who went astray—and one kept safe through God’s guidance. Its implicit question is whether one who must fend off terrible punishment with his face can be like one secure from harm.

The more natural interpretation takes “on the Day of Resurrection” as qualifying “fends off”: the punished person uses his face because his hand, ordinarily used for protection, is shackled to his neck. Others instead take the phrase to mean that a person protects himself in this world from the punishment of Resurrection through Godwariness, in contrast to one persisting in disbelief. Al-Mizan judges this reversal of the first reading overwrought and unnatural.

The angels guarding Hell tell the wrongdoers, “Taste what you used to earn.” Calling them “the wrongdoers” rather than using a pronoun highlights that their worldly wrongdoing (ẓulm) is the cause of their punishment.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that earlier deniers were seized by punishment from a direction they did not expect, so that it came upon them suddenly and without warning—the worst manner of being seized. The verse and those following describe the worldly, humiliating punishment of some disbelievers as an example for others like them.
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains khizy as abasement and humiliation, which God made former deniers taste through punishments such as earthquakes, drowning, being swallowed by the earth, the cry, transformation into animals, or slaughter. The punishment of the Hereafter is surely greater.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains that the Qur’an presents every kind of example so that people may awaken from heedlessness, learn its lesson, and take admonition.
verses.28: Al-Mizan explains ʿiwaj as crookedness or bentness. Qurʾānan ʿArabiyyan is accusative either as praise or special emphasis—“I praise it as an Arabic Qur’an” or “I single it out as an Arabic Qur’an”—or because it functions adverbially with an adjectival meaning.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains the parable as contrasting the idolater with the monotheist. shurakāʾ mutashākisūn are masters who contend through their spiteful character, while salam means belonging wholly to one owner. The idolater resembles a man jointly owned by many rival masters: each claims him, commands what another forbids, and demands exclusive service. The monotheist resembles one wholly owned by a single master, whom he can serve without dispute or confusion.

The two conditions are plainly unequal: service of one master is better than service of many. The parable also subtly evokes the argument of Had there been gods in them other than Allah, they would surely have fallen apart (21:22), against a multiplicity of gods and lords. “All praise belongs to Allah” because serving Him is superior to serving others, though most people do not recognize what should be evident to even slight insight.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that the certainty of death prepares for the certainty that, on the Day of Resurrection, the Prophet and his people—or specifically their idolaters—will dispute before their Lord. According to al-Ṭabrisī, ikhtiṣām is contention between two parties, each rejecting the other’s claim. The Prophet’s complaint is already foretold: And the Messenger will say, ‘O my Lord! Indeed my people consigned this Qur’an to oblivion.’ (25:30)

Although the wording is universal, the following verses indicate that the particular contention concerns the Prophet and the disbelievers of his community.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that the certainty of death prepares for the certainty that, on the Day of Resurrection, the Prophet and his people—or specifically their idolaters—will dispute before their Lord. According to al-Ṭabrisī, ikhtiṣām is contention between two parties, each rejecting the other’s claim. The Prophet’s complaint is already foretold: And the Messenger will say, ‘O my Lord! Indeed my people consigned this Qur’an to oblivion.’ (25:30)

Although the wording is universal, the following verses indicate that the particular contention concerns the Prophet and the disbelievers of his community.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan reads the verse and those following as anticipating God’s Judgment in the Resurrection dispute: the outcome is already determined by whether people acted wrongfully or rightly in this world. The disbeliever’s wrongdoing leads to Hell, while the Godwary and virtuous believer’s conduct leads to Paradise.

The gravest wrong is to fabricate a falsehood about God by ascribing partners and associates to Him and then deny the true message—the divine religion—when the Messenger brings it. The seriousness of wrongdoing corresponds to the rank of the one wronged; therefore wrong against God, and its perpetrator, is greatest. The rhetorical question confirms that Hell is the abode of such faithless people because their arrogant rejection of the truth amounts to lying about God and denying His Messenger’s message.

In context the verse concerns the idolaters contemporary with the Prophet, or those of his own people, but it also applies generally to anyone who introduces an innovation (bidʿa) into religion or abandons an established teaching (sunna).
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains that bringing the truth means bringing the true religion, and confirming it means believing in it; the one who brings it is the Prophet. The plural “they” apparently broadens the description to every prophet who brought and believed in the true religion, and every believer who believes in it and calls others to it. Calling to the truth in word and deed is part of following the Prophet, as in: Say, ‘This is my way. I summon to Allah with insight—I and he who follows me’ (12:108). They are the Godwary.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains that the virtuous will dwell near the Lord in Paradise and receive whatever they wish; there, wishing itself is sufficient for obtaining an object, unlike worldly attainment, which depends on further causes, effort, and assistance. This recompense is due to their virtuousness. iḥsān apparently means righteous deeds, or true belief together with good deeds; hence confirming the true religion requires affirming it in word and deed, not abandoning its ordinances.

If God absolves them of their worst deeds, such as idolatry and major sins, He necessarily absolves lesser sins as well. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, interprets this as sparing them punishment for former idolatry and sins because they have faith, virtuousness, and return to God. Al-Mizan considers this sound: the absolution encompasses evil deeds that are past and followed by faith, virtuousness, and repentance, as an effect of confirming the truth, together with good reward in the Hereafter.

Some commentators hold that God rewards even lesser good deeds according to the measure of the best deeds, with bi aḥsan meaning exchange. Another possible reading is that He assesses the highest degree of their deeds and raises their rank in Paradise accordingly, though this does not fit the parallel absolution of evil deeds. Others take aswaʾ and aḥsan absolutely: every disobedience is worst and every obedience best.
verses.35:

verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains that “others than Him” are the idolaters’ deities, while “His servant” includes first of all the Prophet, the one praised in the preceding verses. “Does not Allah suffice His servant?” is an affirmative assurance that God will protect the Prophet against threats made through those deities, alluding to the promise: Allah shall suffice you against them, and He is the All-hearing, the All-knowing (2:137).

That none can guide one whom Allah leaves astray, and none can mislead one whom Allah guides, are reciprocal universal principles. In this setting, the first assures that those threatening the Prophet will not attain true faith or achieve their aims against him, for God has guided His Messenger and will not let him stray.

“Is not Allah an all-mighty avenger?” is likewise affirmative. His irresistible might and vengeance require retribution against those who obstinately reject truth and persist in disbelief; He therefore leaves them astray without a guide. Conversely, if He guides a servant because of that servant’s Godwariness and virtuousness, no one can lead that servant astray. Thus God’s leading astray is attributed to Him as recompense and punishment for those who have gone astray, not as His causing their initial misguidance.
verses.37:

Thus God’s leading astray is attributed to Him as recompense and punishment for those who have gone astray, not as His causing their initial misguidance.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan argues from the idolaters’ own admission that Allah alone created the heavens and the earth. Since every entity and effect depends on His creation, every good and ill also comes into being by Him; none can prevent a mercy He wills or remove a distress He wills. Governance and the ordering of cosmic affairs belong to creation itself, so the sole Creator necessarily suffices as the sole Lord and God.

The question about “what” they invoke uses mā rather than “whom” so as to embrace both the idols worshipped by most people as gods and the angels or spirits whom some elites regarded as the realities represented by idols. ḍurr, set against raḥma, includes every kind of misfortune; calling them His distress and His mercy explains why others cannot remove or withhold them. The Prophet’s reference to himself suits his dispute with those who threatened him through their deities, while the feminine plural hunna emphasizes the unintelligent idols and supports the inclusion of both idols and their supposed corresponding beings.

“Allah is sufficient for me” is therefore a command to tawakkul: the Prophet practically confirms the lordship established by the proof by trusting Allah in all his affairs. The fronted ʿalayhi in “In Him let all the trusters put their trust” makes this trust exclusive to Him. By using mutawakkilūn, derived from the same root as the verb, the verse praises Allah as uniquely worthy of tawakkul in its authentic sense; those who trust Him are people of insight and cannot be blamed for saying that Allah suffices them.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains makāna as a person’s station and capacity, analogous to how makān is a place for sensible things. The command to the idolaters to act according to their ability thus tells them to persist in their disbelief, obstinacy, and obstruction of God’s way, while the Prophet continues the work commanded to him without turning aside.

It appears that man, “who,” is interrogative: they will learn generally who receives the punishment, not the identity of every individual punished. The disgraceful punishment is worldly punishment, exemplified by Badr, whereas the punishment that descends and remains is the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter. The verse is consequently an exceptionally severe threat.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains makāna as a person’s station and capacity, analogous to how makān is a place for sensible things. The command to the idolaters to act according to their ability thus tells them to persist in their disbelief, obstinacy, and obstruction of God’s way, while the Prophet continues the work commanded to him without turning aside.

It appears that man, “who,” is interrogative: they will learn generally who receives the punishment, not the identity of every individual punished. The disgraceful punishment is worldly punishment, exemplified by Badr, whereas the punishment that descends and remains is the everlasting punishment of the Hereafter. The verse is consequently an exceptionally severe threat.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the Book was sent down “for mankind” so that the Prophet might recite and convey it to them, and “with the truth” means accompanied by truth and free of falsehood. Whoever accepts its guidance gains happiness in this world and the reward of the Hereafter; whoever strays bears his own worldly misery and consequent punishment. God neither benefits from their guidance nor is harmed by their misguidance.

The Prophet is to warn with the Book, but is not charged with watching over people’s affairs or ensuring that Qur’anic guidance enters their hearts, for he has no control over that.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan states that Allah’s being placed before the verb signifies that He alone truly takes souls. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains tawaffā as receiving something completely and in full. The angel of death and the angels mentioned elsewhere are intermediaries acting by God’s command, while the real taking belongs to Him.

Anfus denotes the spirits connected with bodies, not spirits and bodies together. At bodily death, the soul’s connection to the body is severed, so that it can no longer act through or control it. God also takes souls during sleep: if He has decreed death, He retains the soul rather than returning it; otherwise, He returns it to its body, repeatedly if necessary, until its specified term ends. The specified time thus marks the duration for which the soul continues to be released back to the body.

The verse establishes that the soul is distinct from the body and can exist independently when separated from it. Both death and sleep involve God’s taking of the soul, but death is a taking without return, whereas sleep is a taking from which the soul may be returned. These are signs for those who reflect, remembering God’s governance and their return to Him for reckoning.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan takes the initial am as truncated, in the sense of bal: rather, the idolaters have taken their worshipped deities as intercessors with Allah. The rhetorical question rejects this claim. Intercession requires knowledge of what is sought, from whom, and for whom, as well as the power and right to intercede. Thus an inanimate idol cannot intercede.

Nothing possessed by any being besides God is possessed independently of Him; it belongs to Him, and any use of it depends on His permission. The idolaters have neither shown that their deities possess such authority nor that God has authorized them to intercede. Their claim is therefore fabrication: it is foolish to take as intercessors beings which, like angels, have no independent control, or which, like idols, cannot even comprehend anything.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that all intercession belongs to Allah because the kingdom of the heavens and earth belongs to Him. He may grant a servant a limited possession or authority, but no angel or other servant can claim unrestricted intercession; “There is no intercessor, except by His leave” (10:3).

In its deeper sense, the true intercessor is God, and any other intercession occurs only by His permission. Intercession is the mediation of divine attributes between God and the one interceded for, such as mercy and forgiveness rectifying the state of a sinful servant and saving him from sin and punishment. This differs from ordinary ownership, in which what is owned does not share the owner’s quality: in this case, the recipient shares in the master’s quality and is thus described as an intercessor.

Return to God is a further proof that intercession belongs to Him alone: an intercessor must have complete dependence of the recipient and authority to set his affairs right, while no one else has such power except by God’s grant and leave. The worship of deities on the assumption that they will intercede unconditionally is therefore groundless. The commentary rejects readings that make the return merely a threat or merely an assertion of God’s exclusive mastery in the Hereafter, maintaining that it primarily establishes His sole ownership of intercession.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan explains that Allah being mentioned alone means that He is invoked without the idolaters’ gods, as in lā ilāha ill Allāh, “there is no god but God.” Their hearts shrink away—that is, withdraw in aversion—because disbelief in the Hereafter is the root of this response. Had they believed that they would return to God and be recompensed for their deeds, they would have served Him alone rather than false gods.

By contrast, when their deities are mentioned alongside Him, they rejoice with a happiness so intense that its traces appear on their faces.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan holds that the idolaters’ aversion to Allah’s exclusive invocation, arising from their forgetfulness and denial of the Hereafter, shows that no good is to be hoped from continuing the debate. The Prophet is therefore commanded to turn to Allah alone and remind them that He will judge His servants concerning their disagreements.

The invocation both seeks recourse in God and affirms the Resurrection. As Originator, He brought the heavens and earth from non-existence into existence; as Knower of the sensible and the Unseen, nothing is hidden from Him. It follows that He will judge with truth and that His judgment will be executed.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan identifies the wrongdoers as those who deny the Hereafter. If they possessed all the earth’s wealth and its like besides, they would offer it as ransom from the terrible punishment of Resurrection.

What will appear to them from Allah is not simply something they had never believed possible. Badāʾ means coming into sight, while iḥtisāb is counting on something in making one’s plans. Although some use iḥtisāb in the sense of ẓann, al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes them: iḥtisāb adopts one of two opposing possibilities without considering the other, while ẓann considers both and judges one likelier. The deniers had heard of reckoning, the scale, and hell, but, while rejecting them, measured them by familiar worldly realities. When the veil is removed on the Day of Resurrection, they will confront realities far greater, more terrible, and more frightening than they had conceived; what was hidden will become visible.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains that the evils the wrongdoers earned—their evil deeds—will become present to them after having been hidden. They will also be surrounded and afflicted by the very realities they mocked when believers warned them in this world: the hardships and terrors of the Day of Judgment and its various punishments.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan presents this verse as explaining the wrongdoers’ condition: human beings follow the desires of the low self (nafs), are deceived by worldly pleasures and apparent causes, and forget their Lord. When illness or hardship strikes, they pray to Him alone; when He grants them an evident blessing, they forget Him and attribute it to their own knowledge and skill in acquiring wealth.

The contrast between “a blessing from Us” and “I was given it” is deliberate. By using the passive and refusing even to call it a blessing, the recipient detaches it from God and omits its Bestower. The context requires ʿalā ʿilm, “by virtue of knowledge,” to mean by virtue of my own knowledge, not God’s knowledge of the recipient’s worthiness or the recipient’s knowledge that God is pleased with him; those alternatives do not fit the wording.

The blessing is in fact a fitna, a divine test of its recipient, though most do not know it. The interpretations that make the blessing itself a punishment, or make the statement itself the trial, are far-fetched, especially the latter.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that “that” refers to the claim, “I was given it by virtue of knowledge.” The verse refutes it: if blessings came through people’s own cleverness, strength, and earnings, those means would preserve their blessings, prevent loss, and save them from perishing. Yet those before them made the same claim, and their earnings did not avail them; instead, the evil consequences of those earnings struck them.

It appears that those before them refers to Korah and people like him, since he said, “I have indeed been given this because of the knowledge that I have” (28:79).
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that “these” means the Prophet’s own people. The wrongdoers among them will follow the path of earlier wrongdoers: the evil consequences of what they earn will visit them, and they cannot thwart God in the least.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan gives this as a second refutation of the claim that provision is gained by one’s own knowledge, whereas the preceding response exposed that claim’s logical invalidity. Personal effort, knowledge, and will are not sufficient causes of provision; otherwise no seeker would return empty-handed. Provision depends upon innumerable temporal, spatial, and external conditions and impediments whose convergence determines whether effort succeeds.

That convergence is not accidental, for the law governing provision is constant and comprehensive, extending to all living beings and throughout the visible cosmos; were it suspended even for a moment, everything would perish. The unity and harmony of this cosmic order point to the unity of its originator and to a single director and sustainer beyond the world’s constituent parts: God.

Since this order belongs to divine governance, and governance is an extension of creation, the Creator is also the Governor and Provider. “For whomever He wishes” shows that the expansion and tightening of rizq depends on God’s will, not human will. People cannot themselves produce all the means and causes of their provision, nor is provision chance; it follows the cosmic order willed by its Creator and Sustainer, Allah.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains that God commands the Messenger to summon his people on His behalf. By calling them “My servants,” He recalls that they are His servants and He their Master, to whom obedience and worship are due; the possessive “My” also conveys kindness and concern, encouraging them to seek His mercy.

Iṣrāf is exceeding proper bounds, and here means offending one’s own soul by staining it with sins, whether idolatry or major or minor sins. The commentary rejects the view that “My servants” means believers alone. The shared context, culminating in the rebuke of those who denied God’s signs and were faithless, includes idolaters among God’s servants; indeed, the view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that the address specifically concerns idolaters is more plausible. Uses of “My servants” exclusively for believers have contextual indicators, whereas the unqualified expression can include both believers and idolaters.

The mercy that sinners are forbidden to despair of is the Hereafter’s mercy, namely forgiveness. The shift from “My” to “Allah” in “Indeed Allah will forgive all sins” displays that the One offering mercy bears the Beautiful Names, including al-Ghafūr and al-Raḥīm.

Although forgiveness extends to every sin, it is not haphazard but has a cause: intercession or repentance. Since intercession does not include idolatry, while this verse includes idolatry together with all other sins, the promised forgiveness must be forgiveness through tawba. The surrounding verses likewise call servants not to despair, then to repent, submit, and act righteously; thus the verse cannot be detached from its conditions. Al-Mizan consequently rejects both the restriction of its forgiveness to minor sins and the claim of universal, causeless forgiveness excluding idolatry as baseless. Idolatry, like every other sin, can be forgiven through repentance.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains that this command follows the preceding prohibition against despair. Ināba is return to God, or tawba, and the phrase “to your Lord” indicates that His lordship (rubūbiyya) makes worship (ʿibāda) due to Him. To submit to Him is to act in accordance with His will; rather than merely commanding belief, the verse demands the opposite of arrogant refusal of the truth.

The punishment apparently means the punishment of the Hereafter, though it may encompass divine punishment generally. Once such punishment descends, in this world or the next, repentance is no longer accepted; this includes the destruction that befell earlier nations. To receive no help means that forgiveness will not reach them because its cause, repentance, is absent, while intercession does not include their idolatry.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan holds that the command is addressed to all, believers and disbelievers alike, since the Qur’an was sent down for both. Other readings take “the best of what has been sent down” to mean legal rulings rather than narratives; obedience through performing obligatory and recommended acts and avoiding forbidden and disliked ones; the obligatory and forbidden acts alone; or the Qur’an as the best of revealed scriptures. The commentary finds these readings redundant, because “submit to Him” already encompasses them.

Perhaps the intended meaning is instead to follow Qur’anic passages that show how best to fulfil God’s right of servanthood in belief and practice: constant mindfulness of Him, love of Him, wariness of Him as befits Him, and exclusive devotion of faith to Him. Obedience to these summons gives a person a good life, brings the spirit of faith into the heart, rectifies conduct, and places the person under God’s guardianship (wilāya), an unequalled dignity.

The warning of sudden punishment calls for action while the opportunity remains. It exposes the procrastinator who supposes there is still time, and stresses inward rectification as the basis for outward rectification and concrete action.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that tafrīṭ is neglecting a priority until its time has passed, and taḥassur is grief over something no longer obtainable. Janb Allāh, God’s side or vicinity, denotes the obligations owed to Him, such as worshipping Him alone and avoiding disobedience. Negligence in His vicinity is therefore failure to fulfil those duties. The verse warns so that, on the Day of Judgment, no soul will lament having neglected its duties to God and having been among those who ridiculed.
verses.57: Al-Mizan explains that the feminine verb refers to the soul mentioned previously, and that guidance means being shown the right path. The verse forecloses the soul’s excuse on the Day of Resurrection that, had Allah guided it, it would have been among the Godwary.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains that law expresses a wish and that karra, literally a return, is the soul’s wish, upon seeing the punishment on the Day of Judgment, to return to the world and become one of the virtuous.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan takes “Yes, My signs certainly came to you” as God’s rebuke, on the Day of Judgment, of the soul’s claim that it would have been Godwary had Allah guided it. Though the response comes after the third lament about receiving another chance, it answers only the second.

The three laments occur in the order of the guilty people’s passage through that Day. At its onset, when they realize that they are being recompensed for deeds whose time has passed, they regret their negligence and confess that they ridiculed. After they are called to account, the Godwary are sent to paradise and the wrongdoers are ordered apart; then the latter claim that they lacked guidance. Finally, when they are sent to Hell—first seeing it and then entering it—they wish to return to the world and act virtuously.

The placement of the response emphasizes that God singles out the claim of lacking guidance, while not answering the first lament, which is a confession, or the third, which seeks a return to the world. God will rebuke the guilty on the Day of Judgment, prevent them from speaking, and leave their pleas unanswered.
verses.60: Al-Mizan explains that the lies attributed to Allah are claims that He has a partner or a son, as well as innovations in religion (bidʿa). Their gloomy faces signify humiliation, the recompense for their worldly arrogance; hence hell is the abode of the arrogant.
verses.61: Al-Mizan says that mafāza apparently means success, or attaining one’s goal. The bāʾ in “with their triumph” may signify either accompaniment or causation; on the latter reading, the success God decrees for the Godwary is the cause of their deliverance. Their deliverance means that no external harm will touch them and that they will suffer no inward grief.
verses.62: Al-Mizan reads God's creation of all things as the ground for His exclusive governance, lordship, and sovereignty: creation is inseparable from directing what is created. Because every being depends on Him for existence, nothing truly possesses even itself or its effects except through His grant; all are needy, while He alone oversees their affairs. The ownership and agency He grants creatures are themselves parts of His governance, not a delegation that cancels His guardianship. The verse therefore establishes divine oneness in lordship, rather than merely God's self-sufficiency or His preservation of things in existence, readings the commentary finds unsuitable.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains miqālīd as keys to the heavens' and earth's treasuries: their hidden sources, from which beings, provisions, spans, ends, and the course from God and back to Him become manifest. Possessing those keys thus explains why God watches over all things. The statement about those who disbelieve is joined to the preceding declaration that God creates everything: since the argument establishes His exclusive ownership, guardianship, lordship, and divinity, those who reject His signs, oneness, and worship are the losers. The many alternative grammatical linkages offered by commentators have no adequate basis.
verses.64: Al-Mizan takes the verse as the consequence of the proofs that God alone creates, possesses, and governs, and hence alone is Lord and deity. The Prophet's rhetorical question categorically rejects the idolaters' demand that he worship another; the initial placement of ghayr Allāh makes that issue central. Calling them senseless identifies their continued demand, after the signs of divine oneness, as ignorance and folly.
verses.65: Al-Mizan says the rational proof against worshipping others is reinforced by revelation: associating partners with God destroys one's works and makes one a loser. The warning genuinely addresses the Prophet and earlier prophets, showing that the Messenger must himself believe and fulfil the duties to which he calls others; it is not merely an indirect address to his community. Their ʿiṣma does not remove taklīf or free choice: it arises from certain knowledge that prevents sin, as knowledge of poison prevents a person from drinking it while leaving the capacity to do so. Thus commands to an invariably obedient prophet are real and especially emphatic, not formal prohibitions. The losers may specifically be those who deny the signs of God's oneness.
verses.66: Al-Mizan reads bal as turning from the prohibition of worshipping others to the command to worship God instead. The advance placement of Allāh makes the command exclusive: worship Him alone. The fāʾ may be emphatic or mark the consequence of an implicit condition, but the sense remains that worship belongs solely to Him. To be among the grateful is to worship in gratitude for blessings that show His oneness; in its fullest sense, the grateful are the mukhlaṣūn, God's exclusive servants, who devote themselves wholly to Him and use His gifts as He intended.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains qadar, literally measuring, as also denoting rank: the idolaters fail to know God as He should be known because they deny the Resurrection, where every other means and recourse is cut off and His power alone becomes evident. The earth being in His grasp and the heavens in His right hand signify His exclusive power, not a sovereignty newly acquired on that Day; it has always been His, but will then be manifest to all. The scene discloses that no agent exists independently of God, lā muʾaththir fī al-wujūd illā Allāh. Their failure to recognize this leads them to assign governance and worship to associates, whereas God is transcendent above them.
verses.68: Al-Mizan holds that nafakh al-ṣūr is sounded twice, first for death and then for restoration to life; this is supported by Qur'anic evidence and reports from the Prophet's Household, as well as some Sunni reports. Readings that make it three or four soundings are difficult to sustain from the verses; the swooning, ṣaʿiq, belongs with the first sounding because it can mean loss of consciousness and death. Speculations that identify the excepted beings as particular angels have no textual basis, though the exception may concern creatures beyond heaven and earth or, as reports from the Imams suggest, souls that remain when bodies die. At the second blowing people rise from their graves, waiting, looking, or perplexed. Descriptions of terror, emergence, and gathering elsewhere describe successive stages of the Resurrection, not conflicting events.
verses.69: Al-Mizan takes the earth's light in its ordinary sense, not as a direct created light, divine tajallī, or a metaphor for justice; the first has no supporting basis, soundness of reports for the second would not prove it, and the third lacks evidence. It also rejects al-Zamakhsharī's account that nūr here symbolizes truth and justice: the Qur'an supplies no clear instance of nūr meaning truth or conclusive proof, and truth does not simply entail justice. The plausible reading is that the veil of the Unseen is lifted on the Day of Judgment, so realities and the actual forms of good and evil deeds become visible through the light God alone gives after other causal agents have ceased. The earth is specified because its inhabitants' condition is to be revealed and because it rebukes deniers of its Lordship. The Book may mean the accounting, deeds' records, or the Guarded Tablet; prophets are brought concerning their delivery of the message, witnesses testify to deeds, and God judges humankind's disputes without wronging them.
verses.70: Al-Mizan says tawfiya means giving each soul in full what it has done, rather than merely an externally assigned reward; this removes any doubt about the justice of the Judgment announced previously. God needs neither the Book nor prophets and witnesses in order to know deeds, but establishes them as part of a judgment founded on justice. The preceding verse concerns the judgment itself, this verse its execution, and the next its detailed outcome.
verses.71: Al-Mizan explains that the faithless are driven to hell in successive throngs. Its angelic keepers reproach them for having received human messengers who recited the proofs of God's oneness and their duty to worship Him and warned them of this day. They admit that the messengers came but that they denied the signs, so the word of punishment became due against the faithless, as in (2:39). The seven gates are opened for their entry (15:44).
verses.72: Al-Mizan understands the speakers as the angels guarding hell. Their declaration that it is the evil abode of the arrogant identifies the faithless of the preceding verse as those who denied God's signs and obstinately rejected the truth.
verses.73: Al-Mizan treats the omitted consequent after ‘when’ as indicating that paradise's reality exceeds what language can encompass. The Godwary are brought in successive groups, with its gates already opened, and the angels welcome them with peace, blessedness, and everlasting entry. Peace means complete safety from all but what they desire; their blessedness explains both the greeting and their enduring admission.
verses.74: Al-Mizan identifies the speakers as the Godwary praising God for fulfilling His promise, whether the repeatedly revealed promise of paradise, resurrection and reward, or specifically their inheritance of paradise. The last reading makes ‘made us heirs to the earth’ an exposition of that promise: earth means the ground of paradise, and inheritance means that paradise remains theirs alone after others have left the worldly abode or their domination. The verse itself clarifies the intended earth by naming paradise, where they may settle as they wish. Taking earth as this world is senseless unless it means paradise as its ultimate outcome. ‘How excellent is the reward of the doers’ praises those who act for God and may be spoken by the inhabitants of paradise or by God.
verses.75: Al-Mizan describes the Throne as the station from which divine commands governing the cosmos emanate, and the encircling angels as their executors; their appearance makes this order manifest when the heavens are rolled up. ‘Judgment between them’ cannot most naturally mean the angels, who have no dispute, and repeating the earlier human judgment would be unnecessary. Qaḍāʾ can instead denote both the divine verdict and the whole process around it, from resurrection through the respective settlement of hell's inmates and paradise's inhabitants. The final universal praise declares that God has only done, and will do, what is beautiful. It may be uttered by the Godwary, as (10:10) supports, by angels, or by all creatures.
